extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, narratology students, screenwriters, and literature instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Todorov's five-stage model (equilibrium → disruption → recognition → repair → new equilibrium) to analyze or construct short to long-form fictional narratives, and determine genre placement on the uncanny–fantastic–marvellous spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium (initial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stable situation; the world is in balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a readable baseline so the reader can orient. Absence of an initial equilibrium suggests the story 'starts in chaos' and may leave readers unable to orient to the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disruption
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disruption provides the narrative pulse — without it there is 'no narrative pulse.' It should meaningfully disturb the established equilibrium to create stakes and motivate subsequent recognition and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters become aware of the disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is the moment characters register that something is wrong; if missing, characters 'fail to register the disruption (paralysis),' undercutting the narrative's forward movement and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to Repair (agency)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage demonstrates agency and drives plot through attempts, choices, and conflict. A story with 'no repair attempt' lacks agency and may feel inert; the nature and plausibility of repair attempts are evaluative points (creative solutions, failures, moral costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: New Equilibrium (resolution/transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new stable situation, transformed by the events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new equilibrium must be stable and importantly 'not the same as the old one.' The story is the transformation — evaluate how strongly and convincingly the ending differs from the beginning. If absent, there is 'no closure' (open endings can deliberately deny closure but should acknowledge that absence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the Five-Stage Cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Every functional narrative passes through (or deliberately subverts) all five stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether each stage is present or intentionally subverted; deliberate subversion should be recognizable and purposeful rather than accidental omission. Check for consequences of missing stages (e.g., disorientation, lack of pulse, paralysis, absence of agency, lack of closure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation as Core Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must show a genuine transformation: 'the new equilibrium is not the same as the old one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the magnitude and meaning of change between initial and new equilibria. A weak or cosmetic 'change' undermines the claim that the narrative enacted a transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification: uncanny / fantastic / marvellous
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the narrative on Todorov's three-point spectrum: uncanny (rational explanation), fantastic (sustained hesitation), marvellous (supernatural accepted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the handling of apparently supernatural events to classify: if the event is later given a rational explanation → uncanny; if hesitation between natural and supernatural readings is sustained → fantastic; if the supernatural is accepted as real throughout → marvellous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic-specific: sustained moment of hesitation
rubrics_metrics.description: For works of the fantastic, evaluate whether the 'moment of hesitation' is sustained so the reader (and characters) 'cannot decide' between a rational or supernatural explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge craft in maintaining ambiguity without collapsing into explanation or full acceptance. Successful fantastic fiction preserves credible doubt through narrative focus, evidence distribution, point-of-view choices, and refusal to resolve the tension.
